I'm starting student teaching in just over a month (hard to believe it's so close!) and completed my undergrad at one of the top Education programs in the nation. One of the first lessons in my Intro to Education class was about how "there are many ways to be a great teacher". It's different for everyone, and different teachers can be great for different reasons.

Since that's a copout answer, though, here are some of the things I personally try to do in order to be a great teacher:

  • Get to know every student personally. It's harder than you might think. Sure, you'll connect with a couple students right off the bat, and you'll find yourself building gradual relationships with most of the others throughout the year. But there's always going to be those one or two students that kind of slip through, and it's up to the teacher to seek them out and meet them halfway, or more than halfway if necessary. Usually the kids that get looked over are exceedingly average, and in my experience, fairly quiet and reserved. It's not easy to know how to connect to them, but that makes it all the more important, because they probably have even less of an idea how to connect with you. Every kid is important, not just the ones with genius IQs that will probably go on to ivy league schools, and not just the crack babies riding the school-to-prison pipeline.
  • Teach what the kids are interested in. I never realized how much of a struggle this would be until I actually got into the classroom and realized all the bullshit requirements levied on teachers by the administration, school district, and other teachers, not to mention federal and state requirements. You have to be kind of "sneaky" about it - if you're teaching a lesson on narrative writing, allow the kids to write about something that interests them. If you're doing a big research project, let the kids pick their own topics. If a student has an idea for something you didn't explicitly assign, for Christ's sake let them do it, they'll be more excited for it and learn more in the process.
  • Classroom management. It's ambiguous and vague, and there's so many different styles of management and discipline that teachers will defend to their dying breath, but not all management styles are created equal. I've worked with teachers who impose an iron fist in the classroom, waste fifteen minutes lecturing the entire class because of two or three students' actions, and then wonder why they get no respect. I've also worked with teachers who like to joke around and have fun with the kids, but occasionally cross a line and say or do something totally inappropriate. In my extremely humble opinion, good classroom management depends on a healthy balance between reward and punishment, strictness and leniency. I don't claim to know what constitutes a healthy balance, and I expect it will take me years to figure it out, but I know what it isn't, and that's a start.
  • Communicate with parents. Meet them personally if you can. Call them at home or at work if you cannot. Don't wait for a problem with their child to arise before making first contact. Email every parent regularly regarding general updates in the classroom, and it becomes much easier to slip in a note about their child's poor behavior without sounding like a Nazi asshole putting down their perfect little angel. I'm not so naive as to believe bad parent-teacher relationships can be entirely mitigated, because there are some real crazies out there. Most parents, however, love their children and want what's best for them, even if it means admitting that their child can sometimes be a hellion. Be as respectful and professional as possible when dealing with parents, avoid all personal attacks against them or their children, and temper criticisms with compliments (it is possible, every student has strengths). Be the teacher you would want your kid's parent to have if you had to go in for a parent-teacher conference.
  • Have fun. Kids know if you're not enjoying yourself. It's really obvious when a teacher has a bad day, and it's ok that you do, but if that's the norm you probably need to find a different profession immediately. It's your classroom, so if it isn't fun that's entirely on you. When you plan lessons, think back to your own years in school and consider if you, or the average student at your elementary/middle/high school would have enjoyed or at least tolerated the activity. If not, find a more engaging way to teach the lesson. Generally speaking, a classroom will be more fun if there's a good variety of activities. Don't just force the kids to do workbook pages every day, but don't show movies every day either. Again, balance is important.
  • Talk to other teachers. In education, there is no such thing as stealing or plagiarism. Any teacher that doesn't want you to use their lesson plans or is unwilling to share ideas is a straight-up cunt, no exceptions. And if for some reason all of your coworkers are cunts, there are literally billions of ideas online for every lesson, subject, and grade level imaginable.

I wish I could say I abide by these rules all the time, but I'm pretty new at this, and half the time I struggle just to keep that one weird kid in the back of the room from derailing the entire lesson with his weird mouth noises. My goal is to become this teacher by the end of my career, so that in the future when I give out advice like this, I actually have some experience to back it up.

One of the hardest parts of teaching is keeping all the students engaged (every classroom has a wide range of intellect, aptitudes and attention levels). A good teacher can almost always reach one group (brightest, moderate, and slowest students), a great teacher can keep all of the students engaged and interested in the lesson.
